plain_description: Long north–south avenue trunk routes (median 12.58 km, scheduled speed 10.0 km/h) with high weekday demand (~7,018 riders/day, log=8.86), the strongest weekend retention (0.75 of weekday riders) and late-night share (13.7%), moderate peak load per service-hour (32.4 riders/service-hr), low day-to-day volatility (demand_variability=0.175), and the lowest exclusive-stop share (0.447, or 44.7%) because multiple trunk routes share major avenue corridors.

Short, dense crosstown and Select Bus Service corridors (median 4.24 km) carrying high weekday volume (~6,871 riders/day, log=8.84) and the highest peak load in the network (median 65.8 riders/service-hr, double Group 1), with the steadiest weekday demand (demand_variability=0.163), moderate weekend retention (0.54), slow cross-street scheduled speed (9.7 km/h), and 0.500 (50.0%) exclusive-stop share.

Shorter, lower-volume local and commuter-oriented routes (median 4.06 km, ~1,431 weekday riders/day, log=7.27, speed 9.8 km/h) with the sharpest morning peak concentration (34.7% of daily riders in 07:00–09:59), the lowest night share (7.6%) and weekend ratio (0.47), higher day-to-day variability (demand_variability=0.276), and a high share of stops served by no other route (0.691, or 69.1%).

Single outlier route (M35 to Randall's Island, 4.95 km) with the lowest weekday ridership (~146 riders/day in Jan–May, log=4.99), weekend demand exceeding weekday demand (ratio=1.67), the lowest peak riders per service-hour (4.42), the fastest scheduled bridge/island speed (21.7 km/h), the highest demand volatility (demand_variability=0.847), and 1.000 (100.0%) exclusive stops.
Network-wide median across all 41 Manhattan bus routes (Jan–May 2026 training baseline).
